questions.stem: Four hours after a vaginal birth with an epidural, the nurse finds the client's fundus firm, 2 fingerbreadths above the umbilicus and displaced to the right. Lochia is moderate rubra. The client last voided before the epidural was placed. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Help the client to the bathroom to empty the bladder
Massage the fundus until it moves back to midline
Give the prescribed methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM
Document this as expected on the first postpartum day

rationale.correct: A high, displaced fundus suggests bladder distention; have the client void (or catheterize), then reassess the fundus.

perOption.a: A full bladder lifts and displaces the uterus and keeps it from contracting well.
perOption.b: The uterus is firm; emptying the bladder corrects the cause.
perOption.c: The uterus is firm, and the likely cause is the bladder.
perOption.d: A high, displaced fundus is not expected.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: One hour after the birth of a 4.3 kg baby following a 20-hour labor, the client's fundus is soft and boggy 1 cm above the umbilicus, and a pad was saturated in 15 minutes. The pulse is 104/min and the blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg. The bladder is not distended. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Massage the fundus while supporting the lower uterus
Call the provider and request an order for a uterotonic
Raise the client's legs and start oxygen at 10 L/min
Increase the IV rate and draw a hemoglobin level

rationale.correct: Uterine atony is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage; risk factors include a large baby and prolonged labor. Massage first, then uterotonics.

perOption.a: Massage makes the uterus contract and slows bleeding; supporting the lower segment prevents inversion.
perOption.b: The provider is called, but fundal massage comes first.
perOption.c: This treats shock but not the cause of the bleeding.
perOption.d: These follow; stopping the bleeding is first.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A postpartum client with heavy bleeding from uterine atony has a history of preeclampsia and mild intermittent asthma. Current blood pressure is 152/98 mm Hg. Oxytocin is already infusing. Which additional uterotonic order should the nurse question?

options.text: Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM
Misoprostol 800 mcg per rectum
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes
Carboprost 250 mcg IM, with close respiratory monitoring

rationale.correct: Methylergonovine: avoid with hypertension or preeclampsia. Carboprost: avoid or use with caution in asthma.

perOption.a: Methylergonovine causes vasoconstriction and is contraindicated with hypertension or preeclampsia.
perOption.b: Misoprostol is safe with both hypertension and asthma.
perOption.c: This antifibrinolytic is recommended early in postpartum hemorrhage.
perOption.d: Carboprost is used with caution in asthma, but the hypertension makes methylergonovine the clearer contraindication.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing four postpartum clients on the first day after vaginal birth. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: A perineal pad saturated in 15 minutes
Dark red lochia with a few clots smaller than a quarter
Strong cramping that increases during breastfeeding
A firm fundus 1 fingerbreadth below the umbilicus

rationale.correct: Report a pad saturated in 15 minutes, clots larger than a golf ball, a boggy uterus or signs of shock.

perOption.a: This rate of bleeding indicates hemorrhage.
perOption.b: Lochia rubra with small clots is expected for 1 to 3 days.
perOption.c: Oxytocin released during feeding causes afterpains.
perOption.d: This is expected on the first day.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two hours after a rapid forceps-assisted birth, the client's fundus is firm and midline at the umbilicus, and the bladder was emptied 30 minutes ago. A steady trickle of bright red blood continues, and the pulse has risen from 80 to 98/min. Which cause does the nurse suspect?

options.text: A cervical or vaginal laceration
Uterine atony from a tired uterus
Retained fragments of placenta
Normal lochia rubra after birth

rationale.correct: Bleeding with a firm uterus: suspect a laceration or hematoma and notify the provider.

perOption.a: Bright red bleeding with a firm uterus suggests trauma; rapid and forceps births raise the risk.
perOption.b: With atony the uterus is soft and boggy.
perOption.c: Retained tissue usually causes a boggy uterus and later bleeding.
perOption.d: A continuous bright red trickle with a rising pulse is not normal.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On day 3 after a cesarean birth for prolonged labor with ruptured membranes for 26 hours, a client has a temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), a pulse of 112/min, a tender uterus and foul-smelling lochia. The breasts are soft and the incision is dry. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Endometritis
Wound infection at the incision
Mastitis from early breastfeeding
Normal postpartum fever from dehydration

rationale.correct: Endometritis is more common after cesarean birth and prolonged rupture of membranes; it needs IV antibiotics.

perOption.a: Fever, uterine tenderness and foul lochia after a cesarean with prolonged rupture point to infection of the uterine lining.
perOption.b: The incision is dry without signs of infection.
perOption.c: The breasts are soft and not inflamed.
perOption.d: A temperature of 38°C or higher after the first 24 hours suggests infection.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On postpartum day 3, a client cries easily, says, "I don't know why I'm so emotional," and worries about doing things right. The client is feeding and caring for the baby, sleeps when the baby sleeps and denies thoughts of self-harm. What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Explain that baby blues are common and brief, and teach signs of depression
Arrange an urgent psychiatric evaluation before discharge
Suggest the partner take over care of the baby for a few days so the client can rest
Tell the client to try to stay positive for the baby

rationale.correct: Postpartum blues: mild, within 2 weeks. Depression: lasts longer and impairs function. Psychosis: an emergency.

perOption.a: Baby blues affect most new parents and resolve within 2 weeks; teaching the warning signs supports follow-up.
perOption.b: This is not needed for mild, expected blues.
perOption.c: The client is coping and caring for the baby.
perOption.d: This dismisses the client's feelings.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: One week after birth, a client brought in by a partner has not slept for 3 days, paces the room and says, "The voices tell me the baby is evil and has to be stopped." The baby is in a car seat at the client's side. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Have another adult take the baby and stay with the client
Ask the client whether there is a plan to harm the baby
Reassure the client that frightening thoughts are common after birth
Give the prescribed sedative so the client can finally sleep

rationale.correct: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency: ensure infant safety, never leave the client alone with the baby and arrange emergency evaluation.

perOption.a: Postpartum psychosis with command hallucinations about the baby puts the infant in immediate danger.
perOption.b: Assessment follows; the baby is moved to safety first.
perOption.c: Hallucinations are not normal and signal an emergency.
perOption.d: Medicine may follow evaluation, but the infant's safety comes first.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is watching a first-time parent breastfeed a 1-day-old newborn. The parent says the first few sucks were uncomfortable. Which observation shows the newborn is latched on correctly?

options.text: The lips are flanged outward and swallowing can be heard
The baby's cheeks dimple inward with each suck
A clicking sound is heard with each suck
The nipple looks flattened and pinched after the feeding

rationale.correct: Good latch: wide mouth, flanged lips, much of the areola in the mouth, audible swallowing and no pain after the first moments.

perOption.a: A deep latch with audible swallowing shows effective milk transfer.
perOption.b: Dimpled cheeks suggest a shallow latch and poor seal.
perOption.c: Clicking means the baby is breaking the seal.
perOption.d: This shows the nipple was compressed by a shallow latch.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On day 4 after birth, a breastfeeding client has swollen, hard, warm breasts and says the baby has trouble latching. The temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), and there is no redness or lump. What should the nurse suggest?

options.text: Express a little milk to soften the areola before each feeding
Skip feedings on the fullest side until the swelling goes down
Bind the breasts tightly with a snug bra or binder
Feed every 5 to 6 hours to let the milk supply settle

rationale.correct: Engorgement: feed often, soften the areola before latching, warmth before and cold packs after feeding.

perOption.a: Softening the areola helps the baby latch and empty the breast, which relieves engorgement.
perOption.b: Skipping feedings worsens engorgement and lowers supply.
perOption.c: This is for clients who are not breastfeeding.
perOption.d: Feeding 8 to 12 times a day relieves engorgement.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client 3 weeks after birth has a red, wedge-shaped, painful area on the left breast, a temperature of 38.9 °C (102 °F) and body aches. The provider prescribes dicloxacillin. Which instruction should the nurse give about breastfeeding?

options.text: "Keep feeding from both breasts, starting on the sore side."
"Stop breastfeeding until you finish the antibiotics."
"Feed from the right breast and let the left one rest for a week."
"Pump the left breast and throw that milk away."

rationale.correct: Mastitis: keep emptying the breast, rest, fluids, analgesics and antibiotics.

perOption.a: Emptying the breast helps clear the infection, and the milk is safe for the baby.
perOption.b: Stopping leads to milk stasis and can cause an abscess.
perOption.c: The affected breast needs to be emptied.
perOption.d: The milk is safe for a healthy term baby.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: At 1 minute after birth, a term newborn has a heart rate of 110/min, a weak, irregular cry, some flexion of the arms and legs, a grimace when the nose is suctioned and a pink body with blue hands and feet. What Apgar score should the nurse record?

rationale.correct: Heart rate 110 (above 100) = 2. Respiratory effort weak and irregular = 1. Muscle tone some flexion = 1. Reflex irritability grimace = 1. Color acrocyanosis = 1. Total = 6.
references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A term newborn is born vaginally, cries right away and has good tone. The delivery room is 21 °C (70 °F). What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Dry the newborn and place the baby skin to skin
Give the vitamin K injection in the thigh
Weigh and measure the newborn under the radiant warmer
Give the first bath to remove blood and vernix

rationale.correct: First priorities: airway, breathing and warmth; skin-to-skin contact for a stable newborn.

perOption.a: Drying stimulates breathing and prevents heat loss by evaporation.
perOption.b: This can wait until after the first hour.
perOption.c: This can wait; warmth and bonding come first.
perOption.d: Bathing is delayed until the temperature is stable.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize newborn care right after birth.

questions.stem: A parent who plans to breastfeed asks the nurse to skip the newborn's vitamin K shot, saying, "Breast milk has everything the baby needs." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Breast milk is low in vitamin K, so the shot prevents serious bleeding."
"The shot prevents eye infections picked up during birth."
"The shot is a vaccine that protects the baby from the hepatitis B virus."
"The shot helps clear the yellow skin color that some babies develop."

rationale.correct: Newborn medications: vitamin K IM, erythromycin eye ointment and the hepatitis B vaccine.

perOption.a: Newborns have little vitamin K and sterile guts; breast milk is low in it, so the risk of deficiency bleeding is higher.
perOption.b: That is the role of erythromycin eye ointment.
perOption.c: That is the hepatitis B vaccine.
perOption.d: Vitamin K does not treat jaundice.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 2-hour-old newborn weighing 4.4 kg, born to a parent with poorly controlled gestational diabetes, is jittery, feeding poorly and has an axillary temperature of 36.8 °C (98.2 °F). What should the nurse check first?

options.text: A heel-stick blood glucose level
A serum calcium level
A transcutaneous bilirubin level
The newborn hearing screen

rationale.correct: Newborn hypoglycemia: jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy; feed and recheck per protocol.

perOption.a: Infants of diabetic mothers make excess insulin and are at high risk for hypoglycemia.
perOption.b: Hypocalcemia can cause jitteriness, but hypoglycemia is more common and urgent.
perOption.c: Jaundice appears later and does not cause jitteriness at 2 hours.
perOption.d: This is not related to the findings.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A newborn whose parent has type O-positive blood looks yellow on the face and chest at 18 hours of age. The newborn's blood type is A-positive, and feeding is going well. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Report it, because jaundice before 24 hours is pathologic
Document it as physiologic jaundice and keep feeding
Place the crib by a sunny window for a few hours
Switch to formula feeding until the yellow color goes away

rationale.correct: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathologic; physiologic jaundice appears on days 2 to 3.

perOption.a: Early jaundice with an ABO mismatch suggests hemolysis.
perOption.b: Physiologic jaundice appears after 24 hours.
perOption.c: Sunlight is not a safe treatment.
perOption.d: Feeding helps clear bilirubin; stopping breastfeeding is not indicated.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old newborn with hyperbilirubinemia is under phototherapy lights. The nurse observes a new graduate's care. Which action by the new graduate requires correction?

options.text: Covering the eyes with shields and checking under them each shift
Applying lotion to the dry skin on the arms and legs
Changing the newborn's position every 2 to 3 hours
Checking the temperature and counting wet diapers

rationale.correct: Phototherapy: eye shields, maximum skin exposure (diaper only), no lotions, monitor temperature and fluids.

perOption.a: This protects the retinas.
perOption.b: Lotions can cause burns under the lights.
perOption.c: This exposes all of the skin.
perOption.d: Phototherapy raises fluid loss and temperature.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A newborn born at 36 weeks by cesarean birth is 2 hours old. Which findings suggest respiratory distress and need to be reported? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nasal flaring with each breath
Grunting heard at the end of each breath
Retractions between the ribs
A respiratory rate of 72/min at rest
Pauses in breathing of 5 to 10 seconds
Blue hands and feet with a pink trunk
Irregular, abdominal breathing pattern

rationale.correct: Newborn respiratory distress: flaring, grunting, retractions, tachypnea and central cyanosis.

perOption.a: This is a sign of increased work of breathing.
perOption.b: Grunting keeps the alveoli open.
perOption.c: These show increased work of breathing.
perOption.d: A rate above 60/min is tachypnea.
perOption.e: Periodic breathing with pauses under 20 seconds is normal in newborns.
perOption.f: Acrocyanosis is normal in the first days.
perOption.g: Newborns breathe irregularly and mainly with the diaphragm.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is completing a head-to-toe assessment of a 12-hour-old term newborn. Which finding requires follow-up with the provider?

options.text: Bluish color of the lips and tongue
Bluish hands and feet that are cool to touch
Small white bumps across the nose and chin
Blue-gray flat patches on the lower back

rationale.correct: Normal newborn: acrocyanosis, milia, molding, dermal melanocytosis. Abnormal: central cyanosis.

perOption.a: Central cyanosis indicates hypoxemia.
perOption.b: Acrocyanosis is normal in the first days.
perOption.c: Milia are normal.
perOption.d: Congenital dermal melanocytosis is benign.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell normal newborn findings from abnormal ones.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching parents of a 2-day-old newborn about care of the umbilical cord at home. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Keep the cord dry and fold the diaper below it
Apply petroleum jelly around the cord each day
Give tub baths so the cord stays clean
Gently pull the cord off once it turns black

rationale.correct: Cord care: keep it dry, use sponge baths and report redness, odor or discharge.

perOption.a: Dry care promotes separation and prevents infection.
perOption.b: This keeps the cord moist and slows separation.
perOption.c: Sponge baths are recommended until the cord separates.
perOption.d: It falls off on its own in 1 to 3 weeks.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a parent about care of a newborn who had a circumcision with a Plastibell this morning. Which statement by the parent needs correction?

options.text: "I'll call if I see more than a few drops of blood on the diaper."
"A yellowish crust on the tip is part of normal healing."
"I'll take the plastic ring off myself in 2 days."
"I'll call if there is no wet diaper in 12 hours."

rationale.correct: Circumcision: watch for bleeding and voiding; the yellow exudate is normal; do not remove the Plastibell.

perOption.a: This is correct.
perOption.b: Yellow exudate is normal healing.
perOption.c: The ring falls off on its own in 5 to 8 days.
perOption.d: Voiding confirms there is no obstruction.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 2-day-old newborn whose parent used opioids during pregnancy has a high-pitched cry, tremors when undisturbed, frantic sucking on the fists and loose stools. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Swaddle the baby and keep the room quiet and dimly lit
Keep the lights on and play soft music to soothe the baby
Unwrap the baby to reduce sweating and overheating
Feed larger amounts less often to allow longer rest

rationale.correct: Neonatal abstinence syndrome: low stimulation, swaddling, small frequent feeds, rooming-in and medication if needed.

perOption.a: Reducing stimulation calms neonatal opioid withdrawal.
perOption.b: This adds stimulation.
perOption.c: Swaddling is comforting.
perOption.d: Small, frequent feedings are needed.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.
